questions.question: What is a Dockerfile and what are the key instructions?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to write a basic Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application and understand layer-based image building
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not understanding that each instruction creates a layer, leading to inefficient Dockerfiles with many unnecessary layers
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention layer caching and how instruction order affects build performance — placing frequently changing instructions last speeds up rebuilds

questions.direct_answer: A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions to build a Docker image layer by layer. Key instructions include FROM (base image), WORKDIR (working directory), COPY (add files), RUN (execute build commands), EXPOSE (document port), and ENTRYPOINT (startup command). Each instruction creates a new layer in the image.

answer_sections.content:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/my-app.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

A Dockerfile is the recipe for building a Docker image. For a Spring Boot app, a minimal Dockerfile is 5 lines: FROM tells Docker which base image to use — I use eclipse-temurin:17-jre which gives me Java 17's JRE without the full JDK. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the container where we work. COPY brings in the fat JAR that Maven built. EXPOSE documents the port (it doesn't actually open it — that's docker run -p). ENTRYPOINT is the command that runs when a container starts. Docker then builds each instruction as a layer.

follow_up_questions: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in Dockerfile?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: A Dockerfile is a five-line recipe that turns your Spring Boot JAR into something any server in the world can run.

beats.text: A Dockerfile is a plain text file with instructions that Docker reads top-to-bottom to build an image. Each instruction becomes a layer. The result is a portable, self-contained image.

items: FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre — base image with Java 17 JRE already installed
WORKDIR /app — sets the working directory inside the container
COPY target/my-app.jar app.jar — copies the built JAR into the image
EXPOSE 8080 — documents the port (does NOT publish it)
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] — the command that runs when the container starts

beats.text: Notice we use eclipse-temurin:17-jre, not the full JDK image. JRE is enough to run a compiled JAR and results in a much smaller image than bundling the entire JDK.
candidates miss: EXPOSE does not actually open the port. It's documentation. You make the port accessible with -p 8080:8080 in docker run, not EXPOSE.

speakable_v2.cap: Five instructions is all you need for a working Spring Boot Docker image. Everything else is optimization — multi-stage builds, layer caching, smaller base images.

sections.title: Dockerfile: The Blueprint for Container Images
sections.content: A **Dockerfile** is a plain text file that defines how to assemble a Docker image. Think of it as a recipe: you start with a base ingredient (a Linux distribution with Java installed), then add your application JAR, configure the environment, and specify how to run the app. Each line in a Dockerfile creates a new **layer** in the final image, and Docker caches these layers to speed up subsequent builds. For a Spring Boot application, a typical Dockerfile pulls an OpenJDK base image, copies the compiled JAR file into the container, sets environment variables, exposes the application port (usually 8080), and defines the startup command. Understanding **layer caching** is crucial: if you change a line in the Dockerfile, Docker rebuilds that layer and all layers after it. This is why you place instructions that change frequently (like copying your JAR) near the end, and stable instructions (like installing system packages) at the beginning. The result is a portable, self-contained image that runs identically on any system with Docker installed.

sections.title: Spring Boot Dockerfile with Multi-Stage Build
sections.content:
# Stage 1: Build stage
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests

# Stage 2: Runtime stage
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
# Copy only the JAR from build stage
COPY --from=builder /app/target/order-service-0.0.1.jar app.jar
ENV SERVER_PORT=8080
EXPOSE 8080
# Run as non-root user for security
RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S spring -G spring
USER spring:spring
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

sections.title: Key Points
content: **FROM**: specifies the base image to start from, typically eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine for Spring Boot apps to get a minimal Java runtime
**WORKDIR**: sets the working directory inside the container; all subsequent COPY and RUN commands execute relative to this path
**COPY**: transfers files from your local machine (build context) into the image at build time; use COPY target/*.jar app.jar to add your application
**RUN**: executes shell commands during image build, like installing packages or running Maven; each RUN creates a new layer
**EXPOSE**: documents which port the application listens on (metadata only); does not actually publish the port to the host system
**ENTRYPOINT**: defines the command that runs when a container starts from this image; for Spring Boot use ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
**Layer caching**: Docker reuses unchanged layers from previous builds; place frequently changing instructions last to maximize cache hits

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A Dockerfile is basically a script that tells Docker how to build an image for your application. It's just a text file with a bunch of instructions, and each instruction creates a layer in the final image. For a Spring Boot app, you'd start with a FROM instruction to pull a base image that already has Java installed, like eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine. Then you use WORKDIR to set the working directory, maybe to /app, so all your commands run from there. You COPY your JAR file from your local machine into the image. You can run shell commands with RUN, like installing dependencies or setting permissions. EXPOSE documents which port your app listens on, typically 8080 for Spring Boot, but it doesn't actually open the port—that's just documentation. Finally, ENTRYPOINT defines the startup command, which would be something like java -jar app.jar. One thing that trips people up is layer caching. Docker caches each layer, so if you change a line, everything after that line gets rebuilt. That's why you put stable stuff like installing packages at the top and your frequently changing application JAR near the bottom. This way, when you rebuild after a code change, Docker reuses the cached layers for the base image and dependencies, making builds way faster. The big picture is that a Dockerfile turns your Spring Boot application into a self-contained image that runs the same way everywhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between ENTRYPOINT and CMD in a Dockerfile?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of container startup behavior and how to configure flexible vs. fixed container commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using CMD alone when ENTRYPOINT would be more appropriate, or not understanding that arguments passed to docker run replace CMD entirely
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the exec form versus shell form syntax and why exec form is preferred for proper signal handling and PID 1 issues

questions.direct_answer: ENTRYPOINT defines the main executable that always runs when the container starts, while CMD provides default arguments to that executable. If you specify both, CMD becomes the arguments to ENTRYPOINT. CMD can be easily overridden by passing arguments to docker run, but ENTRYPOINT requires the --entrypoint flag to override.

answer_sections.content:
# ENTRYPOINT fixed, CMD provides default args
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=prod"]

# docker run myapp          → java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
# docker run myapp --spring.profiles.active=dev  → CMD overridden

# Spring Boot standard: just ENTRYPOINT
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

ENTRYPOINT is the fixed command that always executes when the container starts — in our case 'java -jar app.jar'. CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT that can be overridden when you run the container. So ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"] with CMD ["--server.port=9090"] means the default is port 9090, but you can override that with docker run myapp --server.port=8080. For most Spring Boot apps I just use ENTRYPOINT without CMD, and pass environment variables like -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod to configure the app.

follow_up_questions: What is the exec form vs shell form in ENTRYPOINT?
How do you pass JVM flags like -Xmx in a Docker ENTRYPOINT?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with configurable startup command
speakable_v2.hook: ENTRYPOINT and CMD look similar but they play different roles — one is the fixed executable, the other is the default argument you can swap at runtime.

groups.heading: ENTRYPOINT
groups.text: Defines the fixed executable that always runs when the container starts. For a Spring Boot app this is always java -jar app.jar. It cannot be overridden by arguments to docker run.

groups.heading: CMD
groups.text: Provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT, or the default command if no ENTRYPOINT is set. CMD can be completely replaced by passing arguments to docker run.

beats.text: ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"] with CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=prod"] means prod is the default. Run docker run myapp --spring.profiles.active=dev and CMD is replaced — but the java -jar part stays fixed.
For most Spring Boot apps, use just ENTRYPOINT and pass configuration via -e environment variables. That's cleaner and avoids confusion about what CMD is overriding.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: if you use the shell form — ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar — Java runs as a child process of sh, so Docker signals like SIGTERM won't reach it cleanly. Always use the exec form with square brackets.

sections.title: Container Startup Commands: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD
sections.content: Both **ENTRYPOINT** and **CMD** control what runs when a container starts, but they serve different purposes. ENTRYPOINT is for the main executable you always want to run — it's the fixed part of your command. CMD provides default arguments to that executable, and these can be easily overridden. Think of ENTRYPOINT as the verb and CMD as the default object: if ENTRYPOINT is java -jar app.jar, CMD might be --spring.profiles.active=dev. When you run the container, you can pass different arguments to replace CMD without changing the main executable. This pattern is powerful for Spring Boot apps because you can bake the java -jar command into ENTRYPOINT and let users provide runtime flags via CMD or docker run arguments.

sections.title: Choosing ENTRYPOINT vs CMD
sections.content: Use **ENTRYPOINT** when you have a fixed main command that should always run — for Spring Boot apps, this is always java -jar yourapp.jar. This prevents users from accidentally overriding your core startup command. Use **CMD** to provide default arguments that users might want to change, like Spring profiles, JVM options, or debug flags. For example, ENTRYPOINT is java -jar app.jar and CMD is --spring.profiles.active=dev. When a developer runs the container in production, they can do docker run myapp --spring.profiles.active=prod and the prod argument replaces the dev default. If you only used CMD for everything, someone could accidentally run docker run myapp echo hello and your Spring Boot app wouldn't even start — the echo command would replace the entire CMD. Combining both gives you safety plus flexibility.

sections.title: ENTRYPOINT and CMD in Practice
sections.content:
# Using ENTRYPOINT with CMD for flexibility
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/customer-service.jar app.jar

# Fixed executable - always runs java -jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Default arguments - can be overridden at runtime
CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=dev"]

# When you run: docker run customer-service
# Executes: java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# When you run: docker run customer-service --spring.profiles.active=prod --debug
# Executes: java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod --debug
# (CMD is replaced by the arguments you provided)

sections.title: Key Points
content: **ENTRYPOINT**: The main command that always executes — use for your core java -jar startup command
**CMD**: Default arguments to ENTRYPOINT or standalone command — easily overridden by docker run arguments
**Exec form**: Use JSON array syntax like ["java", "-jar"] for proper signal handling, not shell form like java -jar
**Combined pattern**: ENTRYPOINT for fixed command plus CMD for default args gives the best flexibility for Spring Boot containers
**Overriding**: docker run arguments replace CMD entirely, but ENTRYPOINT needs --entrypoint flag to change
**Shell vs exec**: Exec form doesn't start a shell, so your Java process is PID 1 and receives signals like SIGTERM properly
**Common use**: ENTRYPOINT for app executable, CMD for environment-specific flags like profiles or JVM options

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: ENTRYPOINT and CMD both control what runs when a container starts, but they're used differently. ENTRYPOINT is the main command that always executes — for a Spring Boot app, that's your java dash-jar command. CMD provides default arguments to that main command, or it's the fallback if there's no ENTRYPOINT. The key difference is how they're overridden. If you pass arguments to docker run, those arguments completely replace CMD but they don't replace ENTRYPOINT — they become additional arguments to it. So let's say your ENTRYPOINT is java dash-jar app.jar and your CMD is dash-dash-spring.profiles.active equals dev. When you run the container normally, it executes java dash-jar app.jar with the dev profile. But if you run docker run myapp dash-dash-spring.profiles.active equals prod, the prod argument replaces the CMD, so now it runs with the prod profile instead. The ENTRYPOINT stays the same. This pattern is really useful because you can bake the core startup command into ENTRYPOINT so users can't accidentally break it, and use CMD for things they might want to customize like profiles or memory settings. One thing to watch out for: always use the exec form with JSON arrays like ["java", "-jar"] instead of shell form. Exec form means your Java process becomes PID 1 and receives signals properly, so docker stop actually shuts down your app gracefully instead of killing it.

questions.question: What is a .dockerignore file and why is it important?

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of build optimization and security basics — excluding unnecessary files from Docker images
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that the entire project directory is sent to Docker daemon by default, including gigabytes of unnecessary files
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that .dockerignore works like .gitignore and that excluding large directories like target/ before rebuild saves significant upload time to the Docker daemon

questions.direct_answer: A .dockerignore file lists files and directories to exclude from the Docker build context. This reduces image size, speeds up builds, and prevents sensitive files from being copied into the image. For Spring Boot apps, you typically exclude target/ class files, node_modules, .git directories, IDE files, and local environment files.

answer_sections.content:
# .dockerignore
target/          # except we COPY target/*.jar explicitly
!target/*.jar    # but keep JARs
.git/            # git history not needed in image
.idea/           # IDE files
*.md             # documentation
src/             # source code (not needed if JAR is pre-built)
Dockerfile       # don't include the Dockerfile itself

items: Docker sends entire build context to Docker daemon before building
.dockerignore prevents sending large/unnecessary files
Reduces build context size → faster build start
Prevents accidentally including secrets in the image
Similar syntax to .gitignore with !/path for negation (include exceptions)

answer_sections.content: When you run docker build, Docker sends the entire current directory to the Docker daemon as a build context. Without .dockerignore, this includes your .git directory with all history, IDE config files, and potentially the whole target/ directory full of compiled files. That can be hundreds of megabytes. .dockerignore works like .gitignore — you list patterns to exclude. For Spring Boot, I exclude everything except the target/*.jar that I need to COPY. This makes builds faster and images smaller. More importantly, it prevents accidentally including secret files like .env in the build context.

follow_up_questions: How do you include a specific file while excluding its parent directory in .dockerignore?
What are the security implications of including .env in a Docker image?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Without .dockerignore, docker build can silently send hundreds of megabytes — including your secrets — to the Docker daemon before a single layer is built.

beats.text: When you run docker build, Docker packages your entire current directory and sends it to the Docker daemon as a build context. This happens before any layer is built. .dockerignore tells Docker what to leave out — using the same syntax as .gitignore.
For a Spring Boot project, the .git directory alone can be tens of megabytes. The target/ folder after a Maven build is even larger. None of that belongs in the image.

items: Exclude .git/ — git history is never needed in a running container
Exclude .idea/ and other IDE files
Exclude src/ if you're copying the pre-built JAR only
Use !target/*.jar to exclude target/ but keep the JAR you need to COPY

beats.text: production trap: accidentally including a .env file in the build context means those secrets end up in the image. Anyone with docker history access or image pull access can read them.

speakable_v2.cap: .dockerignore is a small file with an outsized impact on both build speed and security. Add it to every project alongside the Dockerfile.
followup_handoff: How do you include a specific file while excluding its parent directory in .dockerignore?
What are the security risks of baking secrets into a Docker image?

sections.title: Build Context Filtering with .dockerignore
sections.content: A **.dockerignore** file works exactly like a .gitignore file but for Docker builds. When you run docker build, Docker sends your entire project directory (the **build context**) to the Docker daemon before building the image. Without a .dockerignore file, this includes everything: compiled class files, node_modules, Git history, IDE configuration, local logs, and even your .env files with secrets. This creates three problems: (1) slow builds because gigabytes of unnecessary files are uploaded to the daemon, (2) bloated images containing files that don't belong in production, and (3) security risks if sensitive files leak into the image. A .dockerignore file tells Docker which files and directories to exclude from the build context. For a Spring Boot project, you'd typically ignore the target/ directory since you rebuild the JAR during the Docker build anyway, along with .git, .idea, .env, and *.log files. The syntax uses glob patterns just like .gitignore: target/ excludes a directory, *.log excludes all log files, and !important.txt includes an exception.

sections.title: Typical .dockerignore for Spring Boot Project
sections.content:
# Build output - rebuilt inside Docker
target/
build/
*.class

# Dependencies - managed by Maven/Gradle
node_modules/
.m2/

# Version control
.git/
.gitignore

# IDE files
.idea/
.vscode/
*.iml
.classpath
.project
.settings/

# Environment and secrets - never in image
.env
.env.local
*.key
*.pem
application-local.properties

# Documentation and CI
README.md
Dockerfile*
docker-compose*.yml
.github/

# Logs and temporary files
*.log
*.tmp
.DS_Store

sections.title: Key Points
content: **.dockerignore syntax**: uses glob patterns like *.log for all log files, target/ for directories, and !exception.txt to negate and include a file
**Build context**: the entire directory sent to Docker daemon when you run docker build; without .dockerignore this can be several gigabytes
**Performance impact**: excluding target/ or node_modules can reduce build context from 500MB to 5MB, making builds 10x faster on slow networks
**Security benefit**: prevents accidentally copying .env files, SSH keys, or application-local.properties with database passwords into the image
**Common exclusions**: target/, build/, .git/, node_modules/, IDE files like .idea/, and any local configuration or credential files
**Image size**: a good .dockerignore keeps images lean by preventing temporary files and source code from being copied with COPY . /app
**Placement**: the .dockerignore file must be in the root of the build context directory, next to your Dockerfile

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A .dockerignore file tells Docker which files to exclude when building an image. It works just like a .gitignore file. Here's why it matters. When you run docker build, Docker takes your entire project directory and sends it to the Docker daemon—that's called the build context. If you don't have a .dockerignore, it sends everything: your target folder with compiled classes, your .git history, your node_modules, your IDE files, everything. That's a problem for three reasons. First, it's slow. Uploading a few gigabytes of unnecessary files over the network takes time. Second, it bloats your image. If you do COPY . /app in your Dockerfile, all those files end up in the image. Third, it's a security risk. If you have a .env file with database passwords sitting in your project root, it could get copied into the image. For a Spring Boot project, you'd typically exclude target/ because you're rebuilding the JAR inside Docker anyway. You'd also exclude .git, .idea, node_modules, any .env files, and log files. The syntax is straightforward: target/ excludes a directory, *.log excludes all log files, and you can use an exclamation mark to negate a pattern if you need an exception. The file goes in the same directory as your Dockerfile. A good .dockerignore can cut your build time in half and keep your images clean and secure.

questions.question: How do you pass environment variables to a Spring Boot app running in Docker?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of runtime configuration in containerized Spring Boot applications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding configuration in application.properties instead of using environment variables for container deployment
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Boot converts SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL environment variable to spring.datasource.url property using relaxed binding

questions.direct_answer: Pass environment variables using the -e flag with docker run, like docker run -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders myapp, or define them in the environment section of docker-compose.yml. Spring Boot automatically reads environment variables and uses them to override properties from application.properties or application.yml.

answer_sections.content:
# docker run with env vars
docker run -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/prod \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret \
  myapp:latest

# Or reference from host env file
docker run --env-file .env myapp:latest

items: Spring Boot converts env vars to properties (dots become underscores)
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL → spring.datasource.url (auto-converted)
Environment variables override application.properties values
Never hardcode secrets in Dockerfile or docker-compose.yml
Use Docker secrets or K8s secrets for production credentials

answer_sections.content: Spring Boot's environment variable support is perfect for Docker. Environment variables override application.properties, so I can have a generic image and configure it at runtime. The naming convention: properties like spring.datasource.url become SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL as environment variables — dots become underscores and everything is uppercase. I pass them with -e when doing docker run, or in the environment section of docker-compose.yml for local development. For production, you'd use Docker secrets or Kubernetes secrets rather than plain text env vars, since container inspection can reveal environment variables.

follow_up_questions: What is the 12-factor app methodology and how does it relate to env var configuration?
Why should you not put secrets directly in environment variables in production?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with environment-specific database config
speakable_v2.hook: One Docker image running in dev, staging, and production — environment variables are how you make a single image behave differently in each place.

beats.text: Spring Boot automatically reads environment variables and uses them to override application.properties values. The naming is automatic: dots become underscores and letters go uppercase. So spring.datasource.url in properties becomes SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL as an env var.

Pass -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod and -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/app at docker run time. The same image that ran with an H2 in-memory database in dev now connects to your PostgreSQL in production.

items: docker run -e KEY=VALUE: pass a single environment variable
docker run --env-file .env: load all variables from a file
docker-compose.yml environment section: define per-service variables

beats.text: non-obvious: never hardcode database passwords in your Dockerfile ENV instructions. ENV values in a Dockerfile are baked into the image and visible to anyone who runs docker inspect. Pass secrets at runtime, and for production use Docker secrets or Kubernetes secrets instead of plain env vars.

speakable_v2.cap: The pattern — generic image, runtime configuration via env vars — is the 12-factor app principle. Master it and your Spring Boot apps will deploy cleanly to any environment.
followup_handoff: How do you manage secrets securely in Kubernetes instead of plain environment variables?

sections.title: Runtime Configuration with Environment Variables
sections.content: In containerized deployments, configuration must be external to the image so the same image can run in development, staging, and production with different settings. **Environment variables** are the standard way to pass runtime configuration to a Spring Boot application running in Docker. Spring Boot uses **relaxed binding** to automatically map environment variables to properties: an environment variable named SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL maps to the spring.datasource.url property, overriding any value in application.properties. You can pass environment variables three ways: using the **-e flag** with docker run for individual variables, using **--env-file** to load variables from a file, or defining them in the **environment section** of docker-compose.yml for multi-container setups. This approach follows the **twelve-factor app methodology**, which says configuration should be stored in the environment, not in code. For a Spring Boot app connecting to a database, you'd pass SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL, SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME, and SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD as environment variables, keeping secrets out of your Git repository and allowing the same image to connect to different databases in different environments.

sections.title: Passing Environment Variables to Spring Boot Container
sections.content:
# Method 1: Using docker run with -e flag
docker run -d \
  --name order-service \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=orderuser \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret123 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  order-service:latest

# Method 2: Using --env-file with external file
# File: prod.env contains KEY=value pairs
docker run -d --env-file prod.env order-service:latest

# Method 3: docker-compose.yml for multi-container setup
# version: '3.8'
# services:
#   order-service:
#     image: order-service:latest
#     environment:
#       SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
#       SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Relaxed binding**: Spring Boot converts SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url, SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE to spring.profiles.active using uppercase-underscore format
**Override precedence**: environment variables override application.properties, which overrides application.yml, allowing same image to run in multiple environments
**docker run -e**: passes individual environment variables like -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders for runtime configuration
**--env-file**: loads variables from a file like --env-file prod.env, useful when you have many variables or secrets stored in a secure location
**docker-compose environment**: the environment section in docker-compose.yml defines variables for a service, better for multi-container applications
**Security**: never hardcode passwords in Dockerfile ENV instructions; always pass sensitive values as runtime environment variables or use secrets management
**Twelve-factor app**: this pattern separates configuration from code, making the same Docker image portable across dev, staging, and production

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You pass environment variables to a Spring Boot app in Docker at runtime using the -e flag with docker run. For example, if you need to configure a database connection, you'd run docker run -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=orderuser myapp. Spring Boot automatically picks up these environment variables and maps them to properties. It uses something called relaxed binding, so an environment variable named SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL gets converted to the spring.datasource.url property. This overrides whatever you have in application.properties. If you have a lot of environment variables, you can put them in a file and use the --env-file flag, like docker run --env-file prod.env myapp. That's cleaner than having a dozen -e flags. For multi-container setups, you'd define environment variables in the docker-compose.yml file under the environment section for each service. The key point is that environment variables let you use the same Docker image in different environments. Your dev environment might connect to a local PostgreSQL instance, while production connects to a managed database, but it's the same image. You just pass different environment variables. One mistake freshers make is hardcoding database URLs in application.properties or setting them with ENV in the Dockerfile. That defeats the purpose of containers. You want configuration to be external, so you can deploy the same image everywhere and just change the environment variables.

questions.question: What do the ENV, WORKDIR, and EXPOSE instructions do in a Dockerfile?
questions.title: ENV, WORKDIR, and EXPOSE in Dockerfile
questions.direct_answer: WORKDIR sets the working directory inside the container; all subsequent commands run from this path. ENV sets environment variables available at runtime to the running application. EXPOSE documents which port the application listens on but does not actually publish it — you still need the -p flag with docker run to map the port to the host.

interviewer_intent.testing: Dockerfile literacy — these instructions appear in every real Dockerfile
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking EXPOSE actually publishes or opens the port — it's documentation only; -p flag in docker run publishes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that ENV values set in Dockerfile can be overridden at runtime with docker run -e — good for configuration

sections.title: Understanding WORKDIR, ENV, and EXPOSE Instructions
sections.content: These three Dockerfile instructions handle different aspects of container configuration. **WORKDIR** sets the working directory for all subsequent instructions like RUN, COPY, and CMD; instead of running commands from the root directory, you establish a base path (typically /app) and all operations happen relative to it. **ENV** defines environment variables that persist into the running container, making them available to your application at runtime; you might set ENV JAVA_OPTS="-Xmx512m" to configure JVM memory. **EXPOSE** is pure documentation — it tells users which port the containerized application listens on (like 8080 for Spring Boot) but does not actually publish or open that port. To make the port accessible from outside the container, you must use the **-p flag** with docker run, like -p 8080:8080, which maps the container's port to a host port. A common mistake is thinking EXPOSE alone makes a port accessible; it doesn't. Think of EXPOSE as a label saying 'this app listens on port 8080', and -p as the actual network configuration that routes traffic. ENV variables set in the Dockerfile serve as defaults but can be overridden at runtime with docker run -e, making them useful for configuration that changes between environments.

sections.title: Using WORKDIR, ENV, and EXPOSE in a Spring Boot Dockerfile
sections.content:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine

# Set working directory - all paths now relative to /app
WORKDIR /app

# Environment variables available at runtime
ENV SERVER_PORT=8080 \
    JAVA_OPTS="-Xms256m -Xmx512m" \
    SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=default

# Copy JAR relative to WORKDIR (/app)
COPY target/order-service-0.0.1.jar app.jar

# Document that app listens on port 8080 (metadata only)
EXPOSE 8080

# Commands run from /app directory due to WORKDIR
RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S spring -G spring
USER spring:spring

# Use ENV variable in entrypoint
ENTRYPOINT java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar

# To run: docker run -p 8080:8080 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod order-service

sections.title: Key Points
content: **WORKDIR effect**: sets the current directory for RUN, COPY, ENTRYPOINT, and CMD; using WORKDIR /app means COPY app.jar . places the file at /app/app.jar
**WORKDIR creates directory**: if /app does not exist, WORKDIR /app automatically creates it, so you don't need a separate RUN mkdir command
**ENV persistence**: variables set with ENV are baked into the image and available to the running container; your Spring Boot app can read them
**ENV override**: values from ENV can be overridden at runtime with docker run -e SERVER_PORT=9090, making them useful for default configuration
**EXPOSE is documentation**: EXPOSE 8080 does not publish the port; it's metadata for users; you must use -p 8080:8080 with docker run to map the port
**Multiple ports**: you can EXPOSE multiple ports like EXPOSE 8080 8443 if your app listens on both HTTP and HTTPS
**Best practice**: always set WORKDIR early in the Dockerfile to avoid hardcoding absolute paths in COPY and RUN commands

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These three instructions do different things. WORKDIR sets the working directory inside the container. After you write WORKDIR /app, all your subsequent commands like COPY or RUN execute from that /app directory. It's like doing a cd /app in a shell script. If the directory doesn't exist, Docker creates it for you. This keeps your Dockerfile clean because you don't have to write absolute paths everywhere. ENV sets environment variables that are available to your application when the container runs. For example, ENV SERVER_PORT=8080 sets a variable that your Spring Boot app can read. These are baked into the image, so every container from that image has those variables. But here's the cool part: you can override them at runtime with docker run -e SERVER_PORT=9090. That makes ENV useful for default configuration that you might want to change in different environments. EXPOSE is probably the most misunderstood. EXPOSE 8080 just documents that your app listens on port 8080. It does not actually open or publish the port. It's basically a comment for people using your image. To actually make that port accessible from outside the container, you need to use the -p flag when you run the container, like docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp. That maps the container's 8080 port to the host's 8080 port. Freshers often think EXPOSE alone makes the port work, but it doesn't—you need -p for that.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Three Dockerfile instructions you'll see in every real project — and one of them is purely documentation that does absolutely nothing to the running container.

groups.heading: WORKDIR
groups.text: Sets the current directory inside the container for all instructions that follow. WORKDIR /app means COPY and RUN commands work relative to /app. It's cleaner than using cd in RUN instructions.

groups.heading: ENV
groups.text: Sets environment variables available both during build and at runtime. ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod bakes a default profile into the image, but you can override it with docker run -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev.

groups.heading: EXPOSE
groups.text: Documents which port the application listens on. That's all it does. EXPOSE 8080 does not open port 8080. Port publishing happens at runtime with docker run -p 8080:8080.

beats.text: candidates miss: the most common misconception is that EXPOSE actually opens the port. It doesn't. Think of it as a comment for humans and tooling. The -p flag in docker run is what makes the port reachable.

speakable_v2.cap: WORKDIR keeps your container tidy, ENV lets you configure at runtime, and EXPOSE communicates intent without doing anything. Know which one is which and you'll never confuse an interviewer.
